summary: This informational memo describes a MAPOS extension, the Node Switch Protocol, for automatic node address assignment.

plainLanguage.summary: A host gives each new device on the network an address automatically.

subtitle: Automatic address assignment for MAPOS networks

tldr.problem: In a MAPOS network, each node needs a unique HDLC address based on which switch port it is connected to, but manually assigning these addresses is error-prone and burdensome.
tldr.mechanism: The Node Switch Protocol automates address assignment by having each node send an address request packet to its switch, which replies with an address assignment containing the assigned address.
tldr.outcome: NSP eliminates manual configuration overhead, prevents address collisions, and simplifies node deployment in MAPOS networks.

today: RFC 2173 is an Informational document that describes an extension to MAPOS version 1. It provides practical automation for a protocol stack that was developed for optical networking environments. While MAPOS itself is no longer widely deployed in modern networks, NSP demonstrates a straightforward approach to automatic address provisioning in network segments with simple topologies.

sections.title: MAPOS and Address Assignment
sections.content:
MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH) is a protocol for transmitting network datagrams encapsulated in HDLC frames over optical SONET (Synchronous Optical Network) or SDH (Synchronous Digital Hierarchy) links. In a MAPOS network, SONET switches provide multiple access capability to end nodes.

Each node in a MAPOS network must have a unique HDLC address within a switch. This address is equivalent to the port number of the switch to which the node is connected. In a single-switch environment, the port number directly serves as the address. In a multi-switch environment, the address consists of a switch number and a port number, creating a hierarchical addressing scheme.

The Node Switch Protocol (NSP) provides automatic HDLC address assignment, eliminating the need for manual configuration and preventing address inconsistencies or collisions.
sections.plainLanguage: MAPOS lets computers communicate over fast optical cables controlled by SONET switches. Each computer needs an address that identifies which switch port it is plugged into.

sections.title: Address Formats in MAPOS
sections.content:
MAPOS addresses are 8 bits long, with the least significant bit (LSB) always set to 1, indicating the end of the address field.

In single-switch environments, a unicast address has the most significant bit (MSB) set to 0, with the remaining 7 bits encoding the port number (ranging from 0x01 to 0x7F). Address 0x01 is reserved for the switch's control processor. Broadcast addresses have the MSB set to 1 and all other bits set to 1 (0xFF). Multicast addresses have the MSB set to 1 with the remaining bits indicating a group address.

In multi-switch environments, addresses use variable-length subnet addressing. A unicast address consists of a switch number followed by a port number, both variable-length fields. For example, with 2-bit switch numbers, a node connected to port 0x3 of switch 0x1 would have address 0x23 (binary 00100011). The address 0x01 still represents the local switch's control processor, and addresses of the form 0 followed by switch number and all zeros indicate the control processor of remote switches.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses are 8 bits. If the first bit is 0, it is a regular address (mostly the port number). If the first bit is 1, it is a broadcast or group message. In big networks, part of the address says which switch and part says which port on that switch.

sections.title: The Node Switch Protocol
sections.content:
NSP defines a simple request-reply protocol for automatic address assignment. When a node connects to a MAPOS switch and receives a valid SONET signal, it sends an address request packet to the switch's control processor (destination address 0x01). The NSP packet contains a 32-bit command field (value 1 for address request) and a 32-bit address field (filled with zeros in requests).

Upon receiving an address request, the switch's control processor replies with an address assignment packet. This packet has command value 2, with the assigned address placed in the least significant byte of the 32-bit address field. The remaining bytes are padded with zeros.

If the switch cannot assign an address for any reason, it sends a reject packet (command value 3) with an undefined address field.

If a node does not receive an assignment within 5 seconds, it retransmits the request. Additionally, nodes verify their address every 30 seconds by sending address request packets, which the switch treats as keep-alive signals. If the switch does not receive a request for more than 90 seconds, it assumes the node is down. The switch also assumes a node is down upon detecting a SONET signal failure on that port.
sections.plainLanguage: A new device sends a message saying "I just plugged in, what address should I use?" The switch looks at which port the message came from and sends back "Your address is X." Every 30 seconds, the device asks again to make sure it is still connected.

sections.title: Special Cases: Point-to-Point and Loop-Back
sections.content:
NSP handles two special cases where a switch is not present:

Point-to-point connections occur when two nodes are directly connected without a switch. When a node sends an address request with destination address 0x01 to such a peer, the receiving node recognizes the point-to-point connection by examining the destination address and command. The peer must reply with an address assignment containing the address 0x03. Since both nodes independently send address requests to each other, both obtain address 0x03. This is acceptable because any address may be used in point-to-point mode, and having identical addresses does not cause a problem.

Loop-back connections occur when a node's output port is directly connected to its input port (a diagnostic configuration). The same mechanism as point-to-point applies: the node sends an address request to 0x01, receives its own request, recognizes it as a loop-back, and replies to itself with address 0x03, ultimately obtaining address 0x03 as its configured address.
sections.plainLanguage: If two devices talk directly (no switch between them), they both get the same address and that is fine. If a device sends to itself (a test), the same thing happens.
